analysis.one_liner: Requires FDA safety approval, adverse-event reporting, and batch testing for ephedra diet supplements.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; a year later the FDA banned ephedra supplements on its own.
analysis.plain_summary: Ephedra was an herb sold in weight-loss and energy supplements that had been linked to serious health problems, including deaths. This bill would have required any supplement containing ephedra to get government safety approval before sale, forced makers to investigate and report every report of a death or hospitalization tied to the product, and required testing of each batch to confirm the label's ephedra content. It was introduced in March 2003, sent to a House committee, and never received any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy weight-loss and energy supplements. Under the bill, no ephedra product could be sold until the Health and Human Services Secretary approved it as not posing a significant or unreasonable risk of illness or injury, and makers would have to report serious injuries to the government.

how_it_helps.text: New ephedra supplements would be deemed unsafe — and therefore illegal to sell — unless the Secretary of Health and Human Services approved an application showing the product does not present a significant or unreasonable risk of illness or injury under ordinary conditions of use.

Manufacturers, packers, and distributors would have to investigate every claim of a serious adverse event (death, life-threatening condition, hospitalization, disability, or birth defect) and report to HHS within 30 to 60 days; failing to comply would be a prohibited act under federal food and drug law.

The bill would require regulations forcing testing of every production batch — using high-performance liquid chromatography or an approved method — to make sure the label accurately states how much ephedra alkaloid the product contains, plus expiration dates, retained reserve samples, and lot-number tracking.

It would convert the government's discretionary authority ('may') into a mandatory duty ('shall') to issue good manufacturing practice rules for dietary supplements generally, and make an ephedra supplement misbranded unless its label carries an expiration date.

analysis.who_pays: Companies selling ephedra supplements, and supplement makers generally. Premarket approval applications, batch testing, and adverse-event reporting are costly, and products that could not show safety would have to leave the market.

drawbacks.text: The premarket approval process is modeled on drug approval, which is expensive and slow; an honest supporter would acknowledge it could keep some products off the market or raise their price, and it singles out one ingredient rather than fixing the broader rule that dietary supplements generally reach store shelves without premarket review.

The Health and Human Services Department already had authority to act against unsafe supplements; critics could reasonably argue a new statute was unnecessary, and in fact the FDA later removed ephedra from the market using its existing powers rather than this bill.
Mandatory adverse-event reporting places ongoing paperwork and legal exposure on manufacturers, packers, and distributors whose names appear on labels, even for incidents they did not cause.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a product category that had been tied to deaths and hospitalizations among people taking it for weight loss and athletic performance, and its costs would fall on the companies selling that product. The premarket approval requirement is heavier-handed than supplement regulation generally, but for an ingredient with a documented serious-harm record the trade-off favors consumers. In the end the FDA used its existing authority to ban ephedra in 2004, which achieved much of the bill's core consumer protection without the new approval regime.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; separately, the FDA went ahead and banned ephedra in dietary supplements in 2004 using authority it already had.

narrative.text: Rep. John E. Sweeney introduced the Ephedra Public Protection Act on March 4, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On March 17, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005.
The bill had a total of four cosponsors, three Republicans and one Democrat.

The bill would have classified ephedra supplements as adulterated unless approved in advance by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, imposed adverse-event reporting duties, and required batch testing and expiration dating.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies selling ephedra weight-loss and energy products avoided new approval, testing, and reporting requirements for the life of the Congress. Consumers eventually got protection anyway when the FDA banned ephedra in 2004 under its existing authority, though that came after this bill had already gone nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ephedra supplement sellers; FDA ban came later

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; the bill's sponsorship was small but mixed-party, with a Republican sponsor and cosponsors split three Republicans to one Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would have forced ephedra products through premarket safety approval and mandatory injury reporting, effectively removing products that could not prove safety from the market. The industry's revenue from selling these supplements depended on keeping them on shelves without that burden, which put its interest against the consumers exposed to the product's risks.

By converting the government's 'may' into a 'shall' for good manufacturing practice rules, the bill would have imposed testing and compliance costs across all supplements, not just ephedra. Uniform manufacturing standards also offered the industry a credibility benefit with consumers, so its interest was genuinely two-sided.
